extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters, cub reporters, city editors, and journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for composing newspaper weather stories, rewrites, and follow-up (folo) pieces — how to select angles, structure leads, handle specifics/statistics, avoid pitfalls, and produce effective rewrites and serial follow-ups for local/regional newspapers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison/contrast with the past
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a comparison or contrast with past weather (e.g., past memorable summers) when it fits the extreme weather context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A story comparing the present unpleasantness with that of other years will be read widely because it connects with what readers already are talking about. Prefer comparisons recent enough that many readers can remember and share the remembering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use curious/unusual aspects sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Freakish or curious weather details are usable but must not become the backbone if there is substantial material on other lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freaks of the weather are always usable but can be overdone. If the only thing to say is another instance of 'More of it,' a story built on freak news may be justified; otherwise avoid overemphasis on gimmicks (e.g., 'egg half-fried on sidewalk').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bromidic (clichéd) writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on worn-out phrases and stock weather clichés (e.g., 'Jack Frost paid his first visit').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Old clichés add nothing and mark the writer as unimaginative. Kill ancient clichés (e.g., 'March lamb') and avoid mangled quotations that don't fit the region or audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor language to region
rubrics_metrics.description: Use regional-appropriate language and images; do not use epigrams or sea-based sayings in inland contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A phrase meaningful on the seaboard can be blank in a waterless region. Failure to realize regional weather patterns (e.g., wind direction meanings) reveals a greenhorn reporter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't issue unofficial forecasts presented as fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid asserting your own forecast contrary to the official forecast in a way that could be mistaken for the government's forecast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal law penalizes issuing forecasts in a way that might be mistaken for government's. If you insist on personal optimism, label it as such; expect editors to delete unofficial forecasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fresh, appropriate phrasing and careful word choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Weather copy welcomes new and appropriate phrasings, but picture painting must be effective and each word must fit the image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single wrong word can wreck an otherwise good picture (example: 'wind chattered' is wrong for heavy 60-mph winds). Strive for originality while ensuring accuracy and appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Split long weather coverage into multiple stories
rubrics_metrics.description: When weather coverage expands, consult editors about dividing it into several targeted stories (straight news, roundup, freaks, historical comparison, forecast, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dividing the weather gives each information strand more prominence. Before splitting, ask city/news editors how many splits can be printed and where each will run; otherwise pieces may be pushed inside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cherish and elevate statistics and practical details
rubrics_metrics.description: Use statistics and lists (closed streets, service interruptions, delays) prominently because they hitch directly to reader interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistics belong near the top or in a separate short ruled insert so headline scanners see them immediately. Examples include lists of closed streets or travel detours; place them where readers encounter them quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a separate 'Ruled Insert with Local Weather' for lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Put lists of unavailable streets or similar practical items in a short, separate insert marked for make-up to place at the top of the main story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A ruled insert can be typographically incorporated into the top of the story so readers see essential details almost as soon as they read the headline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be moderate with superlatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid overusing 'the worst,' 'the hottest,' 'the coldest' — young reporters may exaggerate weather extremes that older readers will contest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive superlatives invite reader letters citing more recent worse events; err on the side of caution when labeling events as extremal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use long leads often for weather stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Weather stories often allow and benefit from a long lead (even half a column) followed by a secondary lead and then elaborations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because weather affects many people in many ways, a short stubby lead often fails. Consider separating lead and secondary lead with a picture paragraph to set the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picture paragraph between lead and secondary lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a vivid picture paragraph between the main lead and the secondary lead to separate and enrich the narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An evocative scene (e.g., bus sinking in tar) can serve as an effective buffer and illustration between the main facts and the secondary summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative statements can be preferable in weather copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not force conversion of negative statements into awkward positives; sometimes the negative is clearer and better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'No heat prostrations were reported' is better than the awkward positive 'Residents escaped heat prostrations.' Use clarity over mechanical rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put details readers will ask about high in the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific facts that readers will want first (e.g., exact expected minimum temperature) must appear in the lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterizations like 'even colder tonight' are insufficient; include the specific 'ten to fifteen below' in the lead so readers immediately know the expected severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve secondary/less-essential details for later
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed time-series numbers and minor fluctuations can be foreshadowed in the lead and given full arithmetic lower in the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid stuffing too much numeric minutiae into the lead; give a characterization first and the full details later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide placement of humorous or minor tidbits based on story mood
rubrics_metrics.description: Weigh whether a humorous touch will break the mood of the main story; use it in a side-light or freaks story if it would damage the main tenor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the main story is deeply melancholy, omit the tidbit from the main account; if the main story is only mildly bad, a small humorous tidbit may be left in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify rapidly changing information
rubrics_metrics.description: Because weather conditions and related operational statuses can change quickly, reporters must re-verify earlier information (e.g., road openings) before filing follow-ups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check earlier incomplete items (schools closed, park facilities out of service, street department costs, casualty lists) for updates when preparing folos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the first-day story to list 'incompletes' for folos
rubrics_metrics.description: After the initial account, list items about which information is incomplete so they provide leads for follow-up stories (folo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items such as school closings, park status, or street-department cost estimates make natural follow-ups and should be noted for next-day reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared to revise casualty and casualty-related lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial casualty counts and injury reports often change; expect to update and revise them in folos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Second-day accounting may show additional fatalities or injuries; leave room to amend numbers as investigations and confirmations occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Become a specialist reporter when assigned
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking a regular beat (e.g., weather) makes you the office expert and advances your reporting career.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialist reporters who consistently cover an area rise in experience and standing; take 'the weather as a regular assignment' to become a valued expert.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify clipping piles to prioritize coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: When working rewrites, sort incoming clippings into five piles: kill, future book, rewrite, filler, and follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the kill pile for already-covered items, future book for planned events, rewrite pile for items safe to rewrite, filler for trivial one-sentence rewrites, and follow for ongoing serials needing folos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor readers who saw the morning paper when rewriting
rubrics_metrics.description: When rewriting a morning-paper story for an afternoon paper, favor the audience that already saw the story — make the rewrite seem fresh to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspaper tradition dictates masking the 'old' story so morning-paper readers find a different emphasis. Use new lead, condensation, and angle to achieve alchemy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite rules (five-step standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good rewrite should be (1) shorter, (2) given a new lead, (3) verified, (4) rewritten entirely rather than patched, and (5) better written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shorten substantially (commonly no more than half as long), devise a different emphasis or lead, check names/identifications carefully, avoid piecing old copy to save space, and improve the prose since you have more time than the origin writer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid patching — rewrite entirely for space and freshness
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not save time by tacking a new lead onto the original text; the result will be too familiar and won't save space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete rewrites better conceal the fact the story is twice-told and allow for the necessary condensation and improved writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folo (follow-up) psychology — dig hard for new material
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow-up stories must pump genuinely new information into an old story; editors will demand repeated follow attempts until the story is adequately exhausted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors use folos both as development and as discipline for lazy reporting. Repeated follow orders aim to force reporters to dig deeper until substantial new leads are found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classifications of new information for folos (eight types)
rubrics_metrics.description: A folo's new information usually falls into one of eight categories: new aspect; consequence/result; relation to previous events; reaction; local ends to out-of-town stories; more details; different angle/color; or installment/serial exclusives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories as checklists when chasing folos — e.g., find consequences (death after injury), management reactions, local implications, richer detail, human-interest color, or exclusive serial information to keep the story alive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always tie-in with yesterday in folos
rubrics_metrics.description: Every folo must include a tie-in that presents the essential facts of the original story so readers who missed the first account understand the follow-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If brief, work the tie-in into the lead; if long, run it as the second paragraph. As the story runs multiple days, the tie-in can be shortened progressively.
